claim: Obp59a expression is restricted to the second chamber of the antennal sacculus in Drosophila melanogaster.
source: First, detailed in situ hybridization analysis showed that Obp59a expression is restricted to the second chamber of the antennal sacculus (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1A and described in the text.

claim: Obp59a-GAL4 drives GFP expression restricted to the second chamber of the sacculus.
source: Second, we generated an Obp59a-GAL4 construct, and used it to drive GFP. The expression pattern in the antenna was again restricted to the second chamber of the sacculus (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by GAL4-driven GFP expression data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Obp59a RNA probe labeling coincides with Obp59a-GAL4 driver expression.
source: The labeling produced by the Obp59a probe and by the Obp59a-GAL4 driver coincided (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by double-labeling data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Obp59a-GAL4 shows no expression elsewhere in the fly head or body, or in any of the three larval instars.
source: We found no expression of Obp59a-GAL4 elsewhere in the fly head or body, or in any of the three larval instars.
evidence: Based on experimental observation of Obp59a-GAL4 expression pattern.

claim: Obp59a RNA is expressed only in the adult head according to the Flybase High Throughput Expression Pattern Database.
source: These results are consistent with data from the Flybase High Throughput Expression Pattern Database, which revealed no expression of Obp59a RNA in tissues or developmental stages other than the adult head, which presumably included antennae (Gelbart and Emmert, 2013).
evidence: Supported by reference to Flybase database data.

claim: The tsetse fly Glossina morsitans morsitans diverged from Drosophila melanogaster approximately 75 million years ago.
source: We examined the antenna of the tsetse fly Glossina morsitans morsitans, which diverged from Drosophila melanogaster ~75 million years ago (Wiegmann et al., 2011) and which carries African sleeping sickness.
evidence: Supported by citation to Wiegmann et al., 2011.

claim: Obp59a maps to the sacculus in the tsetse fly Glossina morsitans morsitans.
source: We found that Obp59a again mapped to the sacculus (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data in tsetse fly shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: Obp59a labels cells immediately adjacent to hygrosensitive neurons expressing IR93a-GAL4.
source: IR93a-GAL4 can be seen to label a hygrosensitive neuron in the second chamber (Figure 2, top panel of left column, green; the arrowhead indicates the dendrite). Obp59a labels cells immediately adjacent to this neuron (Figure 2, center and bottom panels, left column).
evidence: Supported by double-label imaging data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Obp59a labels cells adjacent to hygrosensitive neurons expressing IR25a-GAL4, IR40a-GAL4, and IR68a-GAL4.
source: Likewise, IR25a-GAL4, IR40a-GAL4, and IR68a-GAL4 all label hygrosensitive neurons of the second chamber, and in each case, Obp59a labels adjacent cells.
evidence: Supported by double-label imaging data shown in Figure 2.

claim: No axons or dendrites were observed in cells labeled by Obp59a.
source: We did not observe axons or dendrites in any of the cells labeled by Obp59a, consistent with its expression in non-neuronal cells of the sensilla, as expected of an Obp.
evidence: Based on microscopic observation of Obp59a-labeled cells.

claim: Obp59a is expressed in non-neuronal cells of the sensilla.
source: We did not observe axons or dendrites in any of the cells labeled by Obp59a, consistent with its expression in non-neuronal cells of the sensilla, as expected of an Obp.
evidence: Inferred from the absence of neuronal markers in Obp59a-labeled cells.

claim: Obp59a does not label cells adjacent to IR8a-GAL4-expressing neurons.
source: As a negative control, we examined IR8a-GAL4, which does not label hygrosensitive neurons of the second chamber. The neurons it labels are not immediately adjacent to cells labeled by Obp59a (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by double-label imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The anti-Obp59a antibody labels the second chamber of the sacculus.
source: We generated an anti-Obp59a antibody and found that the antibody labels the second chamber of the sacculus (Figure 3A), consistent with that of Obp59a RNA (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The entire Obp59a coding region was deleted using the CRISPR-Cas9 system to generate the Obp59a1 mutant.
source: We deleted the entire Obp59a coding region using the CRISPR-Cas9 system (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Describes the method used to generate the mutant.

claim: The anti-Obp59a antibody does not label the Obp59a1 deletion mutant.
source: When the anti-Obp59a antibody was tested against the antenna of the Obp59a1 deletion mutant, no labeling was observed in the sacculus or anywhere else (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data in mutant shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The anti-Obp59a antibody specifically labels the Obp59a protein.
source: These results indicate that the anti-Obp59a antibody specifically labels the Obp59a protein.
evidence: Inferred from the absence of labeling in Obp59a1 mutant.

claim: No gross morphological defects were observed in the sacculus of the Obp59a mutant.
source: We note moreover that we examined the structure of the sacculus by confocal microscopy and observed no gross morphological defects in the Obp59a mutant (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Obp59a protein is localized within the shafts of hygrosensitive sensilla.
source: The merged images show that Obp59a is in fact found within the shafts of the sensilla, as expected of a protein that is secreted by auxiliary cells of a sensillum into the dendritic lymph (Figure 3I,J) (Pelosi and Maida, 1995).
evidence: Supported by double-labeling data shown in Figure 3I,J.

claim: Obp59a contains a signal sequence.
source: We note that Obp59a contains a signal sequence, consistent with secretion of the protein into the shaft.
evidence: Based on sequence analysis of Obp59a.

claim: Obp59a mutants were backcrossed to the control stock for five generations to minimize genetic background effects.
source: Prior to testing, mutants carrying the Obp59a mutation were backcrossed to the control stock for five generations to minimize genetic background effects.
evidence: Describes the experimental procedure used.

claim: Control flies show rapid hygrotaxis behavior when the inner region is at 70% RH and the outer region is at 20% RH.
source: When the inner region was at 70% relative humidity (RH) and the outer region was at 20% RH, the control flies showed a rapid hygrotaxis behavior: control flies quickly began to move inward toward the more humid region (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Obp59a mutants show little to no change in distribution in the hygrotaxis assay when inner region is at 70% RH and outer region is at 20% RH.
source: By contrast, the distribution of Obp59a mutants showed little if any change.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A striking hygrotaxis phenotype was observed in Obp59a mutants when inner and outer RH were 96% and 20%, respectively.
source: A striking phenotype was also observed when the inner and outer RH were 96% and 20%, respectively (Figure 4C), and 96% v. 70% (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4C and 4D.

claim: Neither control nor Obp59a mutant genotypes show place preference when inner and outer RH are equal at 45%.
source: When inner and outer RH were equal (and set to 45%), neither genotype showed any place preference (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Mutant flies carrying both Obp59a-GAL4 and UAS-Obp59a constructs show stronger hygrotaxis responses than mutant flies carrying either construct alone.
source: We found that when inner and outer RH were 70% and 20%, mutant flies carrying both an Obp59a-GAL4 construct and a UAS-Obp59a construct showed stronger responses than mutant flies carrying either construct alone (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by genetic rescue data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Rescue of hygrotaxis phenotype was observed in the 70% v. 20% and 96% v. 20% RH cases.
source: Rescue was also observed in the 70% v. 20% and 96% v. 20% cases (Figure 4G,H).
evidence: Supported by genetic rescue data shown in Figure 4G,H.

claim: Similar hygrotaxis phenotypes were observed when flies were desiccated prior to the test.
source: Similar hygrotaxis phenotypes were observed when flies were desiccated prior to the test (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: Desiccated Obp59a mutants appear to gravitate toward the more humid region near the end of the test period.
source: We note that the desiccated Obp59a mutants appeared to gravitate toward the more humid region near the end of the test period (e.g. Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The response of desiccated Obp59a mutants gravitating toward humid regions may arise from extreme thirst and perhaps other pathways for humidity detection.
source: This response may arise from extreme thirst and perhaps other pathways for humidity detection (Liu et al., 2007).
evidence: Speculative interpretation with citation to Liu et al., 2007.

claim: The behavior of control flies that were desiccated was not dramatically different from those that were not.
source: We note that the behavior of control flies that were desiccated was not dramatically different from those that were not (Figure 4 vs. Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Comparison of behavioral data in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: An independent allele, Obp59a2, shows a strong hygrotaxis defect in all three test cases: 70% v. 20%, 96% v. 20%, and 96% v. 70% RHs.
source: As further confirmation that the Obp59a gene is required for normal hygrotaxis behavior, we tested an independent allele, Obp59a2, which was also backcrossed five times to the control strain. We again found a strong defect in all three cases: 70% v. 20%, 96% v. 20%, and 96% v. 70% RHs (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–D.

claim: An Obp28a mutant shows no hygrotaxis defects in any test in the Petri dish paradigm.
source: As another control, we tested a mutant of a related gene, Obp28a, which was generated in the same manner as the Obp59a mutants, and found no defects in any test in this paradigm (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E–H).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2E–H.

claim: Following desiccation, Obp59a2 flies show a hygrotaxis phenotype but Obp28a mutant flies do not.
source: We further tested Obp59a2 and Obp28a following desiccation and again found a phenotype for Obp59a2 but not Obp28a (Figure 4—figure supplement 2I–P).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2I–P.

claim: Control flies show a strong preference for high humidity by the first time point (5 min) when given a choice between 70% and 20% RH, and this preference continues for 24 hr.
source: We first gave flies a choice between 70% and 20% RH and found that by the first time point (5 min), control flies showed a strong preference for high humidity; this preference continued for 24 hr (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The response of Obp59a1 was much lower than controls at the first time point in the humidity preference assay, and remained lower over the course of many hours.
source: The response of Obp59a1 was much lower at this first time point, and remained lower over the course of many hours.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Response of Obp59a1 mutant was lower than controls when given a choice between 70% and 50% RH, and between 96% and 70% RH.
source: Response of the mutant was also lower when given a choice between 70% and 50% RH, and between 96% and 70% RH (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: The Obp59a1 mutant retains some limited ability to respond to humidity.
source: The Obp59a1 mutant retains some limited ability to respond to humidity, as evidenced most clearly by the responses in the first two cases at 24 hr, when flies may be very thirsty (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5B,C.

claim: The valence of humidity preference between 96% and 70% RH is dependent on the hydration status of the flies.
source: Knecht et al., 2017 and Perttunen and Salmi, 1956 have shown that the valence of this preference is dependent on the hydration status of the flies, and it is possible that the different preference we have observed in our experiments reflects a difference in the conditions in which the flies are cultured.
evidence: Supported by citations to Knecht et al., 2017 and Perttunen and Salmi, 1956.

claim: The response of Obp59a1 to water vapor in the modified PER test was lower than that of the control genotype.
source: We measured the response of a desiccated fly to the water vapor emanating from a moistened cotton swab. The response of Obp59a1 was lower than that of the control genotype (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Neither control nor Obp59a1 genotypes responded to a dry stimulus in the PER test.
source: Neither genotype responded to a dry stimulus.
evidence: Based on behavioral observations in the PER test.

claim: Anti-IR93a antibody, anti-IR25a antibody, and IR68a-GAL4 driver all labeled neurons in the second chamber of the sacculus of Obp59a1, in a pattern comparable to that observed in controls.
source: We addressed this question with three independent reagents: an anti-IR93a antibody, an anti-IR25a antibody, and an IR68a-GAL4 driver. All three reagents labeled neurons in the second chamber of the sacculus of Obp59a1, in a pattern comparable to that observed in controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry and imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Obp59a1 flies show the same robust climbing behavior as wild type in the RING assay.
source: We tested the ability of Obp59a1 flies to rapidly climb walls in the Rapid Iterative Negative Geotaxis (RING) assay and found that Obp59a1 showed the same robust climbing behavior as wild type (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Obp59a1 shows robust chemosensory responses to an attractive stimulus and several repellent stimuli in an olfactory paradigm.
source: Obp59a1 also shows robust chemosensory responses to an attractive stimulus and several repellent stimuli in an olfactory paradigm (Figure 5H).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The repellent stimuli tested include acetic acid and propionic acid, which are detected at least in part by sensilla in the third chamber of the sacculus.
source: The repellent stimuli include acetic acid and propionic acid, which are detected at least in part by sensilla in the third chamber of the sacculus (Ai et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ai et al., 2013.

claim: Obp59a1 males survived longer than control males under desiccating conditions (0% RH).
source: Remarkably, Obp59a1 males survived longer than control males (Figure 6A, p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by survival data shown in Figure 6A with statistical significance.

claim: Obp59a2 males survived longer than control males under desiccating conditions.
source: Consistent with these results, we found in an independent experiment that Obp59a2 males also survived longer than control males (Figure 6B, p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by survival data shown in Figure 6B with statistical significance.

claim: Obp59a1 and Obp59a2 females survived longer than control females under desiccating conditions.
source: Females survived longer as well, in the case of both Obp59a1 and Obp59a2 (Figure 6C,D, p<0.0001 in both cases).
evidence: Supported by survival data shown in Figure 6C,D with statistical significance.

claim: Survival of males and females of both Obp59a alleles was normal at 70% RH.
source: Survival of males and females of both alleles was normal at 70% RH (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: Supported by survival data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: Obp28a mutants showed normal survival in both males and females at both 0% and 70% RH.
source: As another control, Obp28a mutants showed normal survival, in the case of both males and females and at both 0% and 70% RH (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E–H).
evidence: Supported by survival data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E–H.

claim: The loss of Obp59a leads to an abnormal pattern of humidity signaling, which triggers defensive physiological changes in the fly that protect it from desiccation.
source: One interpretation of these results is that the loss of Obp59a leads to an abnormal pattern of humidity signaling, which triggers defensive physiological changes in the fly that protect it from desiccation.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the desiccation resistance data.

claim: Obp59a is localized within hygrosensory sensilla.
source: We have identified a component essential for normal hygroreception, a critical process about which remarkably little is known. We found that Obp59a is localized within hygrosensory sensilla, and that loss of Obp59a reduced the response of the animal to humidity in three distinct behavioral paradigms.
evidence: Summary statement supported by data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Loss of Obp59a reduced the response of the animal to humidity in three distinct behavioral paradigms.
source: We found that Obp59a is localized within hygrosensory sensilla, and that loss of Obp59a reduced the response of the animal to humidity in three distinct behavioral paradigms.
evidence: Summary statement supported by behavioral data presented in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Animals lacking Obp59a displayed a major increase in resistance to desiccation.
source: Animals lacking Obp59a displayed a major increase in resistance to desiccation.
evidence: Summary statement supported by survival data presented in Figure 6.

claim: Expression of Obp59a in Drosophila is highly localized to the sacculus.
source: Expression of Obp59a in Drosophila is highly localized to the sacculus.
evidence: Summary statement supported by expression data in Figures 1-3.

claim: The tsetse ortholog of Obp59a is also expressed in the sacculus.
source: The tsetse ortholog is also expressed in the sacculus, suggesting that its location has been conserved for at least 75 million years.
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data in tsetse fly shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: The location of Obp59a expression in the sacculus has been conserved for at least 75 million years.
source: The tsetse ortholog is also expressed in the sacculus, suggesting that its location has been conserved for at least 75 million years.
evidence: Inferred from conservation of expression pattern between Drosophila and tsetse fly.

claim: Within the sacculus of Drosophila, Obp59a protein is found in the shafts of hygrosensory sensilla, where dendrites of hygrosensory neurons are located.
source: Within the sacculus of Drosophila the protein is found in the shafts of hygrosensory sensilla, where dendrites of hygrosensory neurons are located (Shanbhag et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 3 and citation to Shanbhag et al., 1999.

claim: Obps are the most abundantly expressed genes in the antenna.
source: Obps are the most abundantly expressed genes in the antenna: in a recent RNAseq analysis, Obp19d and Obp83a were detected at 31,000 and 25,000 RPKM (reads per kilobase per million mapped reads) respectively, while a typical Odor receptor (Or) gene was expressed at ~40 RPKM (Menuz et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to RNAseq data from Menuz et al., 2014.

claim: Obp59a was expressed at approximately 2,000 RPKM.
source: Obp59a was expressed at ~2,000 RPKM, and showed the most highly restricted expression of the antennal Obp genes (Larter et al., 2016): most other Obps are expressed in many more sensilla.
evidence: Supported by citation to Larter et al., 2016.

claim: Obp59a showed the most highly restricted expression of the antennal Obp genes.
source: Obp59a was expressed at ~2,000 RPKM, and showed the most highly restricted expression of the antennal Obp genes (Larter et al., 2016): most other Obps are expressed in many more sensilla.
evidence: Supported by citation to Larter et al., 2016.

claim: The level of Obp59a expression in an individual hygrosensitive sensillum is comparable to that of the most abundantly expressed Obps.
source: These results suggest that the level of Obp59a expression in an individual hygrosensitive sensillum is comparable to that of the most abundantly expressed Obps.
evidence: Inferred from the high RPKM value and restricted expression pattern of Obp59a.

claim: The expression pattern of Obp59a is conserved.
source: Not only is the expression pattern of Obp59a conserved, but its sequence is conserved as well (Stanley and Kulathinal, 2016; Vieira and Rozas, 2011; Zhou et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Stanley and Kulathinal, 2016; Vieira and Rozas, 2011; Zhou et al., 2010.

claim: The sequence of Obp59a is conserved.
source: Not only is the expression pattern of Obp59a conserved, but its sequence is conserved as well (Stanley and Kulathinal, 2016; Vieira and Rozas, 2011; Zhou et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Stanley and Kulathinal, 2016; Vieira and Rozas, 2011; Zhou et al., 2010.

claim: Obp59a is one of only two Obps with clear orthologs across insect orders.
source: Obp59a is one of only two Obps with clear orthologs across insect orders.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about Obp conservation.

claim: The conservation of Obp59a structure suggests that it represents a good solution to a difficult problem that is common to many insects.
source: This conservation suggests that its structure represents a good solution to a difficult problem that is common to many insects.
evidence: Inference based on the high degree of conservation observed.

claim: Antennal Obps are widely believed to transport hydrophobic odorants through the aqueous sensillum lymph to odor receptors in the dendritic membranes of olfactory receptor neurons.
source: Antennal Obps are widely believed to transport hydrophobic odorants through the aqueous sensillum lymph to odor receptors in the dendritic membranes of olfactory receptor neurons (Leal, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Leal, 2013.

claim: An Obp59a mutant was normal in response to both attractant and repellent odorants in behavioral tests.
source: An Obp59a mutant was normal in response to both attractant and repellent odorants in behavioral tests.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Obp59a seems unlikely to carry water molecules across the aqueous lymph to the dendrites of hygrosensory neurons.
source: Obp59a seems unlikely to carry water molecules across the aqueous lymph to the dendrites of hygrosensory neurons.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the nature of water molecules and aqueous environment.

claim: One proposed model for the mechanism of hygroreception is that a change in humidity alters the structure of hygrosensory sensilla, with the structural change being transduced into neuronal responses.
source: One proposed model for the mechanism of hygroreception is that a change in humidity alters the structure of hygrosensory sensilla, with the structural change being transduced into neuronal responses (Altner and Loftus, 1985).
evidence: Supported by citation to Altner and Loftus, 1985.

claim: It is conceivable that Obp59a mutants contain a subtle defect in the structure or composition of the sensillum, and therefore do not undergo a normal structural change in response to changes in humidity.
source: It is conceivable that Obp59a mutants contain a subtle defect in the structure or composition of the sensillum, and therefore do not undergo a normal structural change in response to changes in humidity.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the mutant phenotype.

claim: A role for Obp59a in affecting sensillum structure or composition might fit well with the high abundance of Obp59a within hygrosensory sensilla.
source: Such a role might fit well with the high abundance of Obp59a within hygrosensory sensilla.
evidence: Speculative reasoning connecting abundance to potential function.

claim: Obp59a could possibly affect sensillum structure or composition via a role in transporting hydrophobic components of the cuticular wall of the sensillum.
source: Obp59a could possibly affect sensillum structure or composition via a role in transporting hydrophobic components of the cuticular wall of the sensillum.
evidence: Speculative hypothesis about Obp59a function.

claim: The concept of an alternative role for an antennal Obp is consistent with a recent study showing that the classic odorant-transport model may not apply to all antennal Obps and all olfactory sensilla.
source: The concept of an alternative role for an antennal Obp is consistent with a recent study showing that the classic odorant-transport model may not apply to all antennal Obps and all olfactory sensilla (Larter et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Larter et al., 2016.

claim: When the ab8 sensillum was genetically depleted of its sole abundant Obp (Obp28a), it showed a robust electrophysiological response to odorants; in fact the peak response was increased in many cases.
source: An Obp-to-sensillum map was constructed for all 10 of the abundant Obps, and when one particular sensillum, ab8, was genetically depleted of its sole abundant Obp, it showed a robust electrophysiological response to odorants; in fact the peak response was increased in many cases.
evidence: Supported by citation to Larter et al., 2016.

claim: Obp28a is not required for the transport of odorants to Ors in the ab8 sensillum.
source: These results suggested that Obp28a is not required for the transport of odorants to Ors in the ab8 sensillum.
evidence: Inference from the electrophysiological data cited from Larter et al., 2016.

claim: Antennal Obps do not have a single, unifying function, but rather play diverse roles.
source: Taken together, the results reveal an unexpected molecular component required for normal humidity response. Our findings add further support to the concept that antennal Obps do not have a single, unifying function, but rather play diverse roles.
evidence: Inference based on the findings of this study and previous work.

claim: Obp59a is a new target that could be useful in controlling insect vectors that rely on humidity to find their human hosts and oviposition sites.
source: The results also identify a new target that could be useful in controlling insect vectors that rely on humidity to find their human hosts and oviposition sites.
evidence: Speculative application of the findings.

claim: Deletion of a gene in Drosophila often causes a decrease in fitness.
source: Deletion of a gene in Drosophila often causes a decrease in fitness.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about gene deletions.

claim: A constellation of metabolic changes together produce desiccation resistance.
source: How might greater desiccation resistance be achieved? We suspect that a constellation of metabolic changes together produce desiccation resistance.
evidence: Speculative hypothesis about the mechanism of desiccation resistance.

claim: The pattern of integrated sensory input from all humidity-sensing circuits in the fly is abnormal in Obp59a mutants, which triggers the induction of a defensive state that protects the fly against desiccation.
source: We speculate that owing to the Obp59a defect, the pattern of integrated sensory input from all humidity-sensing circuits in the fly – those activated by the neurons studied here and others (Yao et al., 2005), including other antennal neurons expressing certain Trp channels (Liu et al., 2007) – is abnormal. This abnormality would trigger the induction of a defensive state that protects the fly against the existential threat of desiccation.
evidence: Speculative hypothesis with citations to Yao et al., 2005 and Liu et al., 2007.

claim: Hygroreception is an essential sensory modality that is used to find sources of moisture.
source: Hygrosensation is an essential sensory modality that is used to find sources of moisture.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge.

claim: Hygroreception allows animals to avoid desiccation, an existential threat that is increasing with climate change.
source: Hygroreception allows animals to avoid desiccation, an existential threat that is increasing with climate change.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge and current understanding of climate change impacts.

claim: Mosquitoes use hygroreception to find humans on which to feed, and to find water sources on which to lay eggs.
source: Mosquitoes, for example, use hygroreception to find humans on which to feed, and to find water sources on which to lay eggs (Okal et al., 2013; Takken, 1991).
evidence: Supported by citations to Okal et al., 2013 and Takken, 1991.

claim: Small insects, which have a high ratio of surface area to volume, are especially vulnerable to water loss.
source: Small insects, which have a high ratio of surface area to volume, are especially vulnerable to water loss (Gibbs et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gibbs et al., 2003.

claim: The ability to sense humidity levels may allow an insect to avoid dangerously dry conditions or to initiate physiological changes that protect it against desiccation.
source: The ability to sense humidity levels may allow an insect to avoid dangerously dry conditions or to initiate physiological changes that protect it against desiccation (Stinziano et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stinziano et al., 2015.

claim: The antenna functions as a humidity detector in many insects.
source: The antenna functions as a humidity detector in many insects (Altner and Loftus, 1985; Tichy, 1987; Yokohari, 1978).
evidence: Supported by citations to Altner and Loftus, 1985; Tichy, 1987; Yokohari, 1978.

claim: In the antenna of Drosophila, humidity detection occurs largely in a three-chambered cavity called the sacculus.
source: In the antenna of Drosophila, humidity detection occurs largely in a three-chambered cavity called the sacculus.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about Drosophila anatomy.

claim: The second chamber of the sacculus contains a small number of sensilla that act as hygroreceptors and thermoreceptors.
source: The second chamber of the sacculus contains a small number of sensilla that act as hygroreceptors and thermoreceptors (Enjin et al., 2016; Frank et al., 2017; Kim and Wang, 2016; Knecht et al., 2017; Knecht et al., 2016; Shanbhag et al., 1995; Silbering et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Enjin et al., 2016; Frank et al., 2017; Kim and Wang, 2016; Knecht et al., 2017; Knecht et al., 2016; Shanbhag et al., 1995; Silbering et al., 2011.

claim: These sensilla belong to a morphological class known as coeloconic sensilla, which are small relative to other sensilla.
source: These sensilla belong to a morphological class known as coeloconic sensilla, which are small relative to other sensilla (Shanbhag et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shanbhag et al., 1995.

claim: Four ionotropic receptors expressed in the sacculus (IR93a, IR25a, IR68a, and IR40a) are required for hygrosensation.
source: A major advance was recently made through the discovery that four ionotropic receptors expressed in the sacculus (IR93a, IR25a, IR68a, and IR40a) are required for hygrosensation (Enjin et al., 2016; Frank et al., 2017; Kim and Wang, 2016; Knecht et al., 2017; Knecht et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Enjin et al., 2016; Frank et al., 2017; Kim and Wang, 2016; Knecht et al., 2017; Knecht et al., 2016.

claim: The precise role of these receptors in hygroreception remains unclear.
source: However, the precise role of these receptors in hygroreception remains unclear.
evidence: Statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: The downstream effects of hygrosensory signaling remain poorly understood.
source: Moreover, the downstream effects of hygrosensory signaling remain poorly understood.
evidence: Statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Odorant binding proteins (Obps) are remarkably numerous, extremely abundant, and highly divergent in sequence.
source: Also enigmatic has been a family of small secreted proteins called Odorant binding proteins (Obps). These proteins are remarkably numerous, extremely abundant, and highly divergent in sequence (Graham and Davies, 2002; Hekmat-Scafe et al., 2002; Menuz et al., 2014; Vogt et al., 1989).
evidence: Supported by citations to Graham and Davies, 2002; Hekmat-Scafe et al., 2002; Menuz et al., 2014; Vogt et al., 1989.

claim: There are 52 Obp genes in Drosophila.
source: There are 52 Obp genes in Drosophila, of which 27 were found expressed in the antenna in a recent RNAseq analysis (Larter et al., 2016; Menuz et al., 2014; Younus et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Larter et al., 2016; Menuz et al., 2014; Younus et al., 2014.

claim: 27 Obp genes were found expressed in the antenna in a recent RNAseq analysis.

evidence: Supported by citations to Larter et al., 2016; Menuz et al., 2014; Younus et al., 2014.

claim: Five of the 10 most abundantly expressed genes in the antenna are Obps.
source: Five of the 10 most abundantly expressed genes in the antenna are Obps.
evidence: Draws from RNAseq data cited in the manuscript.

claim: Obps are widely believed to carry odorants to odor receptors in olfactory sensilla.
source: Although Obps are widely believed to carry odorants to odor receptors in olfactory sensilla (Leal, 2013; Leal et al., 2005), there is limited in vivo evidence to support this role (Leal, 2013; Pelosi et al., 2006; Vogt and Riddiford, 1981), and a recent genetic study found that a mutant olfactory sensillum lacking abundant Obps did not show a decreased magnitude of response to a variety of odorants (Larter et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Leal, 2013; Leal et al., 2005.

claim: Obp59a is exceptional in its high degree of sequence conservation among insects.
source: One highly abundant member of the Obp family, Obp59a, is striking in two respects. First, it is exceptional in its high degree of sequence conservation among insects.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about Obp59a conservation.

claim: Unlike nearly all other Drosophila Obps, Obp59a has clear orthologs in a variety of insect orders examined.
source: Unlike nearly all other Drosophila Obps, it has clear orthologs in a variety of insect orders examined (Vieira and Rozas, 2011; Zhou et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Vieira and Rozas, 2011; Zhou et al., 2010.

claim: Obp59a is the most highly localized of the abundant antennal Obps: its expression is restricted to the sacculus.
source: Second, it is the most highly localized of the abundant antennal Obps: its expression is restricted to the sacculus (Larter et al., 2016).
